en.title: Taxation: the whole course
en.short: What a taxation course covers, how it is organised and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What taxation is
sections.text:
Taxation is the study of how the state raises money by compulsory levy, and of the law, accounting and economics around it. A tax is a compulsory payment to government, not a fee for a particular service and not a fine. Students learn who must pay, on what amount, in which country and by when.

The subject sits between law and accounting. The law creates the charge; accounting measures the profit or gain that the law taxes. Economics explains why governments choose one tax over another and what effects that choice has.

These notes are for learning, not professional advice. Rates, thresholds and statutes change and differ by country. Check the current official source: your tax authority, the statute in force and your professional body.

sections.heading: How study is usually organised
sections.text:
In most countries taxation is not a single degree. It is taught as a course or a group of courses inside accounting, business, economics or law degrees, and as a separate paper in professional qualifications. Some institutions offer diplomas or postgraduate degrees in taxation. Check your own handbook for what your award requires.

In Nigeria a BSc in Accounting usually runs four years, and an HND two years after the ND. Taxation appears in these programmes and as a paper of the Chartered Institute of Taxation of Nigeria (CITN), ICAN and ACCA. Ghana, Kenya and South Africa follow similar patterns through ICAG, KASNEB and SAICA.

Lengths, awards and exemption rules differ and change, so confirm them with your school or professional body rather than with a friend’s old notes.

sections.heading: The foundation topics
sections.text:
The course begins with why taxes exist and the principles used to judge them: fairness, certainty, convenience and efficiency. You then study the sources of tax law, how statutes are interpreted, and the constitutional limits on taxing power, including the rule that a tax needs a legal basis.

Next comes administration: registration, returns, assessment, payment and penalties. Income tax fundamentals follow: what counts as income, and the two tests that decide liability, residence and source. Employment income and PAYE come next, then business income and allowable deductions, then capital allowances, which spread the cost of assets over several years.

The foundation ends with indirect taxes such as VAT and sales tax, and with capital gains tax.

sections.heading: The core and advanced topics
sections.text:
The core is computation. You build personal income tax computations with reliefs, then company income tax, then the taxation of partnerships, trusts and estates. Withholding tax and advance tax show how tax is collected during the year rather than only at the end.

The professional topics follow: incentives, audits and assessments, dispute resolution, tax planning and anti-avoidance, and the international rules on residence, source and double taxation. Transfer pricing, tax policy and public finance, property and wealth taxes, customs and excise, digital economy taxation, natural resources and local government taxation complete the picture, with ethics, current and deferred tax in financial statements, and technical writing.

At master’s level the work becomes theoretical and comparative, with advanced international taxation and research methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn a framework and apply it to every tax. Ask: who is the taxpayer? What is the taxable amount? Which country may tax it? When is it due? What relief or credit applies? A computation that answers these in order is easy to mark and easy to check.

Practise with full questions, not by reading answers. Use one layout for every computation, show workings, and reconcile the total back to its parts. Keep a sheet of rates and thresholds, but write the date on it and re-check each figure against the official source before an exam.

Read the statute when a definition matters. Distinguish accounting profit from taxable profit at every step.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
The most common error is to treat one country’s rules as universal. Residence rules, rates and reliefs are national. Say which country you mean.

Other frequent mistakes:
Using a rate or threshold from an old year.
Confusing accounting profit with taxable profit, or deducting capital spending instead of claiming capital allowances.
Mixing up residence and source, or forgetting that a treaty may override domestic law.
Ignoring withholding tax already deducted, so the tax is paid twice.
Treating tax avoidance and tax evasion as the same thing.
Writing an answer with no workings, so a small arithmetic slip loses all the marks.

keyPoints: A tax is a compulsory payment to government created by law, not a fee for a service.
Residence and source are the two tests that decide which country may tax a person’s income.
Accounting profit and taxable profit are different, and the difference must be explained.
Capital spending is usually relieved through capital allowances, not deducted like a business expense.
Tax rules belong to one country and one year, so name the country and check the current statute.
Show your workings in every computation, because a right answer without them earns few marks.

en.title: Nature, purposes and principles of taxation
en.short: Definition, purposes, distinctions, tax bases, rate structures and the classic canons.

sections.heading: What a tax is
sections.text: A tax is a compulsory payment to government. It is not a payment for a specific service or direct benefit. This separates tax from a fee, charged for a particular service and often set to cover its cost; a fine, a penalty for breaking a law; a royalty, paid for the right to use a resource or property; and a user charge, a price for using a public facility. The line can blur, but the legal basis differs.

sections.heading: Purposes of taxation
sections.text: Taxes raise revenue for public spending. They can redistribute income by taking more from higher-income groups and funding services for others. They regulate behaviour: a tax on tobacco or carbon can discourage harmful activity, while reliefs can encourage saving. They can support representation: the link between paying tax and holding government to account is old, expressed in the slogan 'no taxation without representation'. That slogan came from American colonial protests against British rule. Modern accountability depends on many institutions.

sections.heading: Base, rates and canons
sections.text:
The tax base is the amount on which tax is charged: income, consumption, property or wealth. A rate structure sets how tax changes as the base rises. A direct tax is levied on a person or firm. An indirect tax is levied on goods or services and can be passed on in prices. A progressive tax takes a rising share as the base rises; a proportional tax takes a constant share; a regressive tax takes a falling share.

Worked example: bands of 0% on the first 200,000, 10% on the next 300,000 and 20% above 500,000. For income 800,000, tax = 0 + 30,000 + 60,000 = 90,000. Average rate = 90,000 ÷ 800,000 = 11.25%. Marginal rate = 20%. A flat 10% gives 80,000 on 800,000, average 10%. A fixed 20,000 charge is 5% of 400,000 but 2.5% of 800,000, so regressive.

Adam Smith’s canons: equity, certainty, convenience and economy, meaning fairness, clear rules, convenient payment and low collection cost.

keyPoints: A tax is compulsory and not a direct payment for a specific benefit.
Taxes raise revenue, redistribute income, regulate behaviour and can support representation.
A fee pays for a service, a fine punishes an offence, a royalty pays for resource use, and a user charge prices a public facility.
Average tax rate = tax ÷ tax base; marginal tax rate = tax on the next unit of base.
Progressive taxes take a rising share, proportional taxes a constant share, and regressive taxes a falling share.
Adam Smith’s canons are equity, certainty, convenience and economy.

en.title: Tax law: sources, interpretation and constitutional limits
en.short: This summary covers where tax law comes from, how courts read it, and the limits on taxing power.

sections.heading: Sources and hierarchy
sections.text: Tax law starts with the constitution, which prevails over other law. Primary legislation means Acts or statutes passed by the legislature. Delegated legislation, such as regulations made under an Act, has force only within that Act. Case law is judicial interpretation; in common-law systems it binds lower courts in the same jurisdiction. Tax treaties allocate taxing rights between countries; in many countries a treaty applies domestically only when incorporated by statute, so check the country. Circulars and practice notes explain how an authority applies the law. They guide officials and may create legitimate expectations, but courts need not follow them.

sections.heading: Reading the words
sections.text: Courts use several approaches. The literal rule gives words their ordinary meaning, even if the result seems harsh. The golden rule starts literally but avoids absurdity or inconsistency. The mischief rule asks what problem the statute was passed to cure and reads it to cure that problem. The purposive approach asks what the law aims to achieve and interprets it in that light. The approaches overlap. A court reads the statute as a whole and may use explanatory material where the law allows. Tax charges must be clear; ambiguities are often read in the taxpayer’s favour, but this varies by country.

sections.heading: Limits and boundaries
sections.text: Constitutional limits vary. A common principle is legality: a tax needs clear legal authority, usually in a statute, and officials cannot invent a charge. Other limits may include equality, property rights, privacy and fair hearing. Taxpayer rights commonly include notice, reasons, objection and appeal, representation and confidentiality, but details are country-specific. Avoidance and evasion differ. Avoidance is arranging affairs to reduce tax within the law, such as structuring a transaction to exploit a gap in the rules. Evasion is illegal, such as hiding income or claiming false deductions. In a made-up case, Ada fails to declare income. That is evasion, not avoidance. General anti-avoidance rules may counter artificial schemes where a country has them.

keyPoints: Constitutions prevail over statutes, and delegated legislation must stay within its enabling Act.
Case law interprets statutes and, in common-law systems, binds lower courts in the same jurisdiction.
Circulars and practice notes guide administration but are not primary law.
Literal, golden, mischief and purposive approaches are tools of interpretation, not rigid separate rules.
The legality principle requires clear legal authority for every tax.
Avoidance uses the law to reduce tax; evasion involves illegality such as concealment or false claims.

en.title: Tax administration and compliance
en.short: How tax authorities register taxpayers, assess returns, collect tax, and handle disputes and penalties.

sections.heading: Authorities and registration
sections.text: Tax administration is the system that registers taxpayers, receives returns, assesses and collects tax, and resolves disputes. The tax authority is the body created by law to do this. Examples include the Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS) and state internal revenue services in Nigeria, the South African Revenue Service (SARS), the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA), HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) in the United Kingdom, and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) in the United States. Taxpayer registration gives a tax identification number (TIN). Rules and names change, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: Tax year and returns
sections.text: The tax year is the period for which tax is computed. It may be the calendar year, a fixed year such as 6 April to 5 April in the United Kingdom, or a company’s accounting period. A return is the formal statement of income, deductions and tax due. Under self-assessment, the taxpayer calculates the tax and pays it, but the authority may later check or audit the return. An assessment is the authority’s official calculation of tax, often made when no return is filed or the return is questioned. Payment must be made by the date in the law or notice.

sections.heading: Records, disputes and penalties
sections.text: Record keeping means keeping books, invoices, receipts and bank records for the period the law requires. Good records support the return and any objection. An objection is a formal written challenge to an assessment, made within the time limit. If it fails, the taxpayer may appeal to a tax tribunal or court. Penalties and interest may apply for late filing, late payment or an incorrect return. Limitation periods set the maximum time for raising an assessment or collecting tax; the law also sets deadlines for objections and appeals and rules on how long records must be kept. These periods differ by country, so check the current official rules.

sections.heading: Amina’s case
sections.text: Case: Amina in Kano registers for a TIN, files her return and keeps receipts. When an assessment seems too high, she objects in writing before the deadline, using her records.

keyPoints: Tax administration covers registration, returns, assessment, payment and disputes.
A tax authority is the body created by law to administer taxes, such as FIRS in Nigeria or SARS in South Africa.
The tax year is the period used to compute tax; it may be a calendar year or another period.
Self-assessment means the taxpayer computes and pays tax, subject to later verification.
Keep records for the required period; they support returns and objections.
Objections, appeals, penalties and limitation periods follow current law and differ by country.

en.title: Income tax fundamentals: income, residence and source
en.short: Taxable persons, income versus capital, residence, source and a simple taxable income computation.

sections.heading: Who and what is taxed
sections.text: Income tax is charged on taxable persons: the people and entities a country’s law taxes, such as individuals, companies and trusts. The law also decides which receipts are income and which are capital. Income usually comes from work, trade, rent or interest. Capital comes from selling an asset, such as land or shares, and is often taxed separately as capital gains. The tax base is the amount on which tax is charged, normally taxable income. Definitions and rates vary by country, so check local law.

sections.heading: Residence and source
sections.text: Residence and source decide whether a country taxes a person and which income it taxes. Residence is usually based on presence in the country for a set number of days, on domicile (your permanent legal home) or on a permanent home there. Source is where the income arises, such as work done in a country or property located there. A resident may be taxed on worldwide income; a non-resident may be taxed only on income from sources in that country. The tax year is the annual period used for assessment. Dates vary by country.

sections.heading: Building taxable income
sections.text: Start with total receipts. Remove capital receipts and exempt income. The remaining income receipts form gross income. Then subtract allowable deductions: expenses incurred in producing the income and permitted by law. The result is taxable income. Suppose a trader has receipts of 500,000, including 80,000 from selling a machine. Allowable deductions are 120,000. Taxable income = 500,000 − 80,000 − 120,000 = 300,000. If the illustrative rate is 20%, tax = 300,000 × 20% = 60,000.

sections.heading: Rates and reliefs
sections.text: Rates may be progressive, where the rate rises with income, or flat, where one rate applies. Individuals often have progressive rates and companies a flat rate, but this varies. Deductions reduce income before tax. Allowances and reliefs may reduce taxable income or the tax payable, depending on the law. They are not the same as deductions. Apply the rules of the relevant country and tax year.

keyPoints: Taxable persons are those a country’s law charges; income is taxed, while capital is often taxed separately.
Residence and source determine whether and on what income a person is taxed.
Taxable income = total receipts − capital and exempt receipts − allowable deductions.
Tax = taxable income × applicable rate; progressive rates rise with income, flat rates do not.
Deductions reduce income, while allowances and reliefs may reduce taxable income or tax payable.
The tax year and all detailed rules vary by country, so check current local law.

en.title: Employment income and PAYE
en.short: Employee versus self-employed, taxable pay and benefits, and how employers withhold and remit PAYE.

sections.heading: Employee or self-employed
sections.text: An employee works under a contract of service; a self-employed person works under a contract for services. Courts look at substance, not labels: who controls the work, whether the worker must do it personally, whether they carry financial risk and supply their own tools. Employees normally have tax withheld by the employer under PAYE, pay as you earn. The self-employed are taxed on business profits and file their own returns. Wrong status shifts tax and social contributions.

sections.heading: Cash pay and benefits
sections.text: Employment income covers salary, wages, bonuses, commissions, allowances and tips. Benefits in kind, such as a car, housing or a cheap loan, are usually taxable too, valued by statutory rules like a percentage of cost. Some benefits, such as medical cover, are exempt or capped. Employees can deduct little: normally only contributions to an approved pension scheme and a few statutory reliefs. Personal costs such as commuting are not deductible. Rates and rules differ by country and year.

sections.heading: PAYE and employer returns
sections.text: PAYE is a withholding system. The employer deducts tax each payday, remits it to the revenue authority by a monthly deadline, and files an annual return. It also issues the employee a certificate of pay and tax (P60 in the UK, P9 in Kenya). In Nigeria the employer’s annual return is Form G. At year end tax deducted is reconciled with tax due on actual income, giving a refund or a balance. Forms and deadlines change, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Hypothetical country and rates, to show the mechanics only.
Annual salary 4,800,000
Car benefit 600,000
Pension contribution, 8% of salary = 384,000
Taxable income = 4,800,000 + 600,000 − 384,000 = 5,016,000
Tax: first 2,000,000 at 10% = 200,000
Next 3,016,000 at 20% = 603,200
Total tax = 803,200
Monthly PAYE = 803,200 ÷ 12 = 66,933
Average rate on taxable income = 803,200 ÷ 5,016,000 = 16.0%
A year-end bonus would raise tax, and reconciliation would collect the extra.

keyPoints: An employee works under a contract of service and has tax withheld under PAYE; a self-employed person is taxed on business profits.
Taxable employment income = cash pay + taxable benefits in kind − allowable deductions.
Employees can deduct only what the law allows, usually approved pension contributions and a few reliefs.
The employer withholds PAYE each payday, remits it monthly and files an annual return.
End-of-year reconciliation compares tax deducted with tax due and produces a refund or extra tax.
Rates, bands, benefit valuations and deadlines differ by country and change often; check the current official source.

en.title: Business income, allowable deductions and losses
en.short: Trading profits, allowable deductions, depreciation, losses, basis periods, stock and bad debts.

sections.heading: Trading profit and timing
sections.text:
Business income is profit from a trade, profession or vocation. Trading profit is sales revenue less the cost of goods sold and allowable running expenses. In Nigeria, company profits are taxed mainly under the Companies Income Tax Act (CITA), as amended; individuals and partnerships fall under the Personal Income Tax Act (PITA), as amended. From January 2026, Nigeria’s main tax laws, including CITA and PITA, are consolidated in the Nigeria Tax Act 2025. Check the current statute.

Timing follows an accounting basis. The accrual basis records income when earned and expenses when incurred; the cash basis records them when received or paid. Tax law may require one basis. A basis period is the period whose profits are taxed in a year of assessment (the tax year); it is often the accounting year, but the statute controls.

sections.heading: Deductible and capital items
sections.text:
An allowable deduction is expenditure incurred wholly, reasonably, exclusively and necessarily for the purpose of the business, of a revenue (operating) nature and not banned by statute. Non-deductible items include private or domestic spending, fines and penalties, general provisions, and accounting depreciation. Capital expenditure buys or improves a lasting asset; it is not deducted as an expense but may attract capital allowances.

Closing stock is normally valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (expected selling price less costs to sell). Bad debts are deductible only when a specific debt is written off as irrecoverable; a general provision is not.

sections.heading: Losses and worked check
sections.text:
A trading loss arises when allowable expenses exceed income. Loss relief rules differ: many systems carry trading losses forward against future profits, while carry-back or group relief is limited. In Nigeria, company trading losses are generally carried forward, subject to CITA.

Worked example. A company has accounting profit of ₦150,000. Expenses include depreciation ₦30,000, a general bad-debt provision ₦10,000 and a fine ₦5,000. All three are non-deductible. Adjusted profit = 150,000 + 30,000 + 10,000 + 5,000 = ₦195,000. A specific bad debt written off is deductible, so it is not added back. Capital allowances would be deducted after this figure.

keyPoints: Trading profit = sales revenue − cost of sales − allowable expenses.
Adjusted profit = accounting profit + non-deductible expenses − non-taxable income.
Accrual basis records income when earned; cash basis records it when received.
Capital expenditure and depreciation are not deducted; capital allowances may apply separately.
Specific bad debts written off are deductible; general provisions are not.
Trading losses usually carry forward; check the country’s statute.

en.title: Capital allowances and tax depreciation
en.short: How tax law gives deductions for capital assets, using initial and annual allowances and balancing adjustments.

sections.heading: Capital expenditure and tax depreciation
sections.text: In Nigeria, companies do not deduct capital expenditure as a business expense. Instead, the Companies Income Tax Act (CITA) and its First Schedule grant capital allowances. These are the tax version of depreciation. Accounting depreciation is usually added back in the tax computation. Only qualifying assets used in the trade qualify. From 2026, the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 replaces CITA. Check the current law, Finance Acts and FIRS guidance, because rates and rules change.

sections.heading: Allowances and rates
sections.text: In Nigeria, capital allowances are worked out asset by asset, not in pools; some other countries group assets into pools instead. Asset classes include plant and machinery, motor vehicles, furniture and industrial buildings. Each qualifying asset starts at its cost. Some assets also get an initial allowance in the first year. The annual allowance is the current rate times the tax written-down value. Rates differ by class and are set by law; do not assume one rate for all assets. Confirm the current percentages in the First Schedule to CITA. The balance after allowances is the tax written-down value.

sections.heading: Balancing adjustments and incentives
sections.text: On sale, compare the proceeds with the asset’s tax written-down value. If proceeds exceed the tax written-down value, the excess is a balancing charge and increases taxable profit. If proceeds are less, the shortfall is a balancing allowance. Investment incentives can accelerate relief, for example higher initial allowances for mining, or an investment allowance. These are separate from the normal annual allowance; check current law.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A company buys plant for ₦1,000,000. Assume the annual rate is 25% and there is no initial allowance. Year 1 allowance = 25% × 1,000,000 = ₦250,000. Tax written-down value = 1,000,000 − 250,000 = ₦750,000. It sells the plant for ₦900,000. Balancing charge = 900,000 − 750,000 = ₦150,000. Check: net relief = 250,000 − 150,000 = ₦100,000, which equals cost 1,000,000 − sale 900,000. Replace the assumed figures with the current official rates, including any initial allowance.

keyPoints: Capital expenditure is relieved by capital allowances, not by deducting the purchase price.
Annual allowance = rate × tax written-down value.
Tax written-down value is cost less allowances made to date.
If sale proceeds exceed the tax written-down value, the excess is a balancing charge.
A balancing allowance arises when proceeds are below the tax written-down value.
Rates and investment incentives differ by country and asset class; check current law.

en.title: Indirect taxes: VAT and sales tax
en.short: How VAT and sales tax work: taxable supplies, input and output tax, registration, exemptions, invoices and returns.

sections.heading: The basic mechanics
sections.text:
An indirect tax is charged on spending, not on income. The seller collects it from the buyer and passes it to the tax authority, so the real burden falls on the final consumer.

VAT (value added tax, called GST, goods and services tax, in some countries) is charged at each stage of the chain. A business charges output tax on its sales and pays input tax on its purchases, then sends the difference to the state. Sales tax is normally charged once, often at the point of sale to the consumer or at manufacture.

A taxable supply is a supply of goods or services made in the course of business for a consideration (payment in money or in kind), within the scope of the tax. A registered business is a taxable person.

sections.heading: Registration and invoices
sections.text:
A business must register once its turnover passes the threshold set by law. The threshold, the rate and the filing dates differ by country and are changed by annual finance laws, so check the current statute and the tax authority’s guidance rather than relying on an old figure.

A registered business must charge the correct tax, issue a tax invoice showing its registration number, the parties, the description, the rate and the tax amount, keep records for the required period, and file periodic returns, usually monthly or quarterly, paying by the due date. A valid invoice is what supports a customer’s claim for input tax.

sections.heading: Exempt and zero-rated
sections.text:
Zero-rated supplies are taxable at 0%. The seller charges nothing but can still recover input tax. Exports are commonly zero-rated so goods are not taxed twice across borders.

Exempt supplies fall outside the tax. No output tax is charged, and input tax on costs used to make them cannot be recovered, so it becomes a real cost. Typical exemptions include some basic foods, medical, educational and financial services, but the list is country-specific.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Assume a standard rate of 10%. A trader buys goods for 40,000 plus input tax of 4,000. She sells part for 70,000 plus output tax of 7,000, and exports part for 20,000, zero-rated.

Output tax = 7,000 + 0 = 7,000.
Input tax = 4,000, all recoverable because both sales are taxable supplies.
Net tax payable = 7,000 − 4,000 = 3,000.

If 10,000 of the purchases had instead been used for exempt sales, input tax of 1,000 would be blocked. Recoverable input tax falls to 3,000, and the payment rises to 7,000 − 3,000 = 4,000.

keyPoints: VAT is charged at each stage with credit for input tax; sales tax is normally charged once.
Net tax payable = output tax − recoverable input tax.
Zero-rated sales carry 0% but allow input tax recovery; exempt sales do not.
Registration is compulsory above a turnover threshold that differs by country.
A valid tax invoice is the evidence for claiming input tax.
Rates, thresholds, exemptions and deadlines change, so check the current law and official guidance.

en.title: Capital gains tax
en.short: Chargeable assets, disposals, computation, exemptions, reliefs and rates under Nigeria’s CGTA.

sections.heading: What CGT taxes
sections.text: Capital gains tax (CGT) is a tax on the gain made when a chargeable asset is disposed of. A chargeable asset is property that the law includes in the tax, such as land, buildings, shares and other investments. A disposal happens on a sale, gift or exchange, and the Act treats loss or destruction of the asset as a disposal. The gain is not the whole sale price. It is the excess of the sale price over what the asset cost. In Nigeria, the Capital Gains Tax Act (CGTA) sets out the rules. Some assets and gains are exempt; the Act lists them, so always check the current version.

sections.heading: Computing the gain
sections.text:
The basic formula is: Gain = Disposal proceeds − Cost base. The cost base is what the asset cost to acquire, plus incidental costs of buying and selling, such as legal fees and stamp duty. If the proceeds are less than the cost base, the result is a capital loss. In Nigeria, capital losses cannot be set against gains; the CGTA gives no relief for them. Rollover relief allows a gain to be deferred when business assets are replaced. The gain is deducted from the cost of the new asset, so it is taxed later.

Worked example: A machine bought for ₦2,000,000. Incidental purchase costs ₦100,000. Sold for ₦2,800,000. Selling costs ₦150,000.
Cost base = 2,000,000 + 100,000 = 2,100,000.
Net proceeds = 2,800,000 − 150,000 = 2,650,000.
Gain = 2,650,000 − 2,100,000 = 550,000.
Tax at 10% = 55,000.

sections.heading: Rates and administration
sections.text: In Nigeria, the CGTA imposes tax at 10% of the chargeable gain. This rate can be changed by a Finance Act, so confirm the current rate. FIRS administers CGT for companies, and state internal revenue services administer it for individuals. Taxpayers must include capital gains in their tax returns and pay within the required time. Penalties apply for late filing or payment. Other countries have their own CGT rules, rates and reliefs. Always use the statute of the country concerned.

keyPoints: CGT taxes the gain on disposal of chargeable assets, not the whole sale price.
Gain = disposal proceeds − cost base (acquisition cost plus incidental costs).
A capital loss arises when proceeds are less than the cost base; in Nigeria it cannot be set against gains.
Rollover relief defers a gain when business assets are replaced.
In Nigeria, the CGTA sets the rate at 10%, but check the current Finance Act.
In Nigeria, FIRS administers CGT for companies and state revenue services for individuals; other countries have their own rules.

en.title: Personal income tax computation and reliefs
en.short: Aggregating income, applying reliefs and bands, credits and returns, with a checked example.

sections.heading: Aggregating income
sections.text: Personal income tax usually begins with total income from all taxable sources. Add employment income (salary, wages and benefits), business profit after allowable deductions, investment income (interest, rent, dividends) and other taxable receipts. Residence and source rules decide what is included; those rules are covered elsewhere. Keep each source separate in your working so you can check it. Total income is not the same as taxable income.

sections.heading: Reliefs, bands and credits
sections.text: Reliefs reduce income before tax rates apply. Examples are pension contributions, personal allowances and dependant allowances. Taxable income = total income − reliefs. Bands then tax slices of taxable income at progressive rates. The marginal rate applies to the next unit of income; the effective rate is tax ÷ total income. A credit reduces the tax itself, not income. A non-refundable credit cannot create a refund; a refundable one can. Rules and rates differ by country and year, so use the current official schedule.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Figures in units. Employment 4,000,000; business profit 1,200,000; investment 300,000; other 100,000. Total income = 4,000,000 + 1,200,000 + 300,000 + 100,000 = 5,600,000. Reliefs: pension 400,000 and personal allowance 600,000. Taxable income = 5,600,000 − 1,000,000 = 4,600,000. Illustrative bands: first 1,000,000 at 10%; next 2,000,000 at 15%; next 2,000,000 at 20%. Tax = (1,000,000 × 10%) + (2,000,000 × 15%) + (1,600,000 × 20%) = 100,000 + 300,000 + 320,000 = 720,000. Credit for employment tax already paid = 150,000. Tax payable = 720,000 − 150,000 = 570,000. Effective rate on total income = 720,000 ÷ 5,600,000 = 12.86%.

sections.heading: Returns and checks
sections.text: An annual return reports each income source, reliefs claimed, credits and tax already paid. Many countries use self-assessment, where the taxpayer calculates the liability and files by a deadline. Keep receipts, pension records and employment tax certificates. Check the arithmetic and current official rates, bands and reliefs for your country and tax year. If tax paid exceeds the liability, claim a refund only if the law allows.

keyPoints: Total income = employment income + business profit + investment income + other taxable income.
Taxable income = total income − reliefs.
Tax = sum of each band slice × its rate.
Tax payable = tax − credits.
Effective rate = tax ÷ total income; the marginal rate applies to the next unit of income.
Rates, bands, reliefs and credits vary by country and year, so use the current official schedule and keep records for the return.

en.title: Company or corporate income tax
en.short: Taxable profits, capital allowances, losses, distributions, returns and minimum tax for companies.

sections.heading: Taxable profit
sections.text: Company income tax, or corporate tax, is charged on the taxable profits of a company. Taxable profit starts with accounting profit and is adjusted. Add back expenses the law does not allow, such as fines, and deduct income that is exempt. Depreciation is not deducted; capital allowances replace it. The main statute in Nigeria has been the Companies Income Tax Act (CITA), as amended by Finance Acts; from 1 January 2026 the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 replaces it. Other countries have their own company tax statutes, so always use the current one.

sections.heading: Capital allowances and losses
sections.text: A capital allowance is tax relief for qualifying capital expenditure, such as plant and machinery. It is claimed instead of accounting depreciation, usually over several years. Trading losses are generally relieved against profits of the same or later years, but rules on carry-forward periods and ownership changes vary. Check the statute. Where a company has no taxable profit, some countries impose a minimum tax or alternative charge. Nigerian law has a minimum tax for certain companies, with exemptions; rates and thresholds change.

sections.heading: Distributions and returns
sections.text: Distributions, usually dividends, are paid out of after-tax profits. They are not a deduction in computing taxable profit. Dividends may also attract withholding tax, which is a separate topic. Companies must file an annual self-assessment return with the tax authority, usually with accounts and a computation, and pay the tax due. Rates differ by country, company size and year. In Nigeria, the rate depends on company size under the current law; do not rely on an old rate.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A company has accounting profit 5,000,000. Add back depreciation 800,000 and a non-deductible fine 200,000. Deduct capital allowance 1,000,000. Taxable profit = 5,000,000 + 800,000 + 200,000 − 1,000,000 = 5,000,000. If a 500,000 loss is brought forward, taxable profit = 4,500,000. At an assumed 30% rate, tax = 4,500,000 × 30% = 1,350,000. The 30% is only for this example; use the current statutory rate.

keyPoints: Taxable profit = accounting profit + disallowed expenses − exempt income − capital allowances − loss relief.
Tax = taxable profit × the statutory rate.
Depreciation is not deducted; capital allowances take its place.
Distributions are not deductible, and they may face withholding tax.
Companies file a self-assessment return and pay the tax due.
Minimum tax or alternative charges may apply where there is no taxable profit; rates and exemptions vary by country and year.

en.title: Taxation of partnerships, trusts and estates
en.short: How partnership profits, trust income and estate income are allocated and taxed.

sections.heading: Partnership basics
sections.text: A partnership is a business owned by two or more partners. In many tax systems it is not taxed as a company. It files an information return showing income, expenses and each partner’s share. Each partner reports that share on a personal return and pays tax at personal rates. The partnership agreement sets salaries, interest on capital and the profit-sharing ratio. If it is silent, the default rule is set by each country’s law, so check the current statute. Losses are allocated in the same way, but relief may be limited in some countries, for example by basis or at-risk rules.

sections.heading: Worked allocation
sections.text: A and B share residual profits 2:1. Partnership profit is 120,000. Salary: A 24,000, B 12,000. Interest on capital: A 6,000, B 3,000. Residual = 120,000 − 24,000 − 12,000 − 6,000 − 3,000 = 75,000. A gets 75,000 × 2/3 = 50,000; B gets 25,000. A total = 24,000 + 6,000 + 50,000 = 80,000. B total = 12,000 + 3,000 + 25,000 = 40,000. Check: 80,000 + 40,000 = 120,000. Each partner includes these amounts in taxable income; the partnership normally pays no income tax.

sections.heading: Trusts and settlements
sections.text: A trust is created when a settlor transfers assets to trustees, who hold them for beneficiaries. A settlement is the arrangement itself. Tax treatment varies. In a conduit system, income is taxed in beneficiaries’ hands when distributed; in others the trust is a separate taxpayer. Trustees may file a return. Distributions can carry tax credits. Accumulated income may be taxed to the trust. Check current law for rates, exemptions and reporting.

sections.heading: Estates
sections.text: When a person dies, an executor or administrator collects assets and pays debts. During administration, the estate may be a separate taxpayer. Income earned by the estate is reported by the estate, or by beneficiaries when distributed, depending on local law. The final return and distribution rules differ, so confirm deadlines and forms with the tax authority.

keyPoints: A partnership usually files an information return, while partners report their shares and pay tax at personal rates.
Allocate profit by agreement: salaries and interest first, then residual in the profit-sharing ratio.
Partner’s total share = salary + interest on capital + residual share.
Losses follow the same allocation but relief may be limited in some countries, for example by basis or at-risk rules.
Trust income may be taxed to the trust or to beneficiaries, depending on the country and whether income is distributed.
Estate income during administration may be taxed to the estate or to beneficiaries; check current local law.

en.title: Withholding tax and advance tax
en.short: How withholding and advance tax are deducted, credited, remitted and checked.

sections.heading: What the taxes are
sections.text: Withholding tax (WHT) is income tax collected at source by the payer. The payer deducts a set percentage from a payment and remits it to the revenue authority. It is common on dividends, interest, rent, service fees and contract payments. Advance tax is tax paid before the final assessment, often in instalments based on estimated income. Terminology varies: some countries treat WHT as a form of advance tax, while others make certain WHT final.

sections.heading: Credits and exemptions
sections.text: WHT is usually a credit against the recipient’s final income tax. The recipient includes the gross payment in taxable income, computes tax, then subtracts WHT already paid. If credits exceed the liability, a refund may be due. Some WHT is final, so no further credit arises. Exemptions and reduced rates differ by country, payment type, recipient residence and tax treaties. Check the current official schedule: for example, Nigeria’s FIRS (renamed the Nigeria Revenue Service from 2026), Kenya’s KRA or South Africa’s SARS. Do not assume a rate from another country.

sections.heading: Remittance and compliance
sections.text: The payer must deduct at the correct rate, remit within the prescribed period, file the required return and issue a withholding certificate to the recipient. Records must show gross amount, rate, tax deducted, net paid and remittance evidence. Late remittance can attract penalties and interest. Recipients should reconcile certificates with their tax returns. Advance tax instalments must be estimated carefully; underpayment may lead to penalties, while overpayment ties up cash until refund.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Illustrative figures, not a real rate. A company pays a resident contractor 500,000 for services. WHT rate is 5%. WHT = 500,000 × 5% = 25,000. Net paid = 500,000 − 25,000 = 475,000. The payer remits 25,000 and issues a certificate. The contractor includes 500,000 in income. If final tax is 60,000, credit = 25,000, balance payable = 60,000 − 25,000 = 35,000. If WHT were final, no credit would arise.

keyPoints: Withholding tax is deducted at source by the payer and remitted to the revenue authority.
WHT is often a credit against final tax: balance = final tax − WHT credits.
Some WHT is final; check the country’s current rules.
WHT = gross payment × rate; net paid = gross − WHT.
Advance tax is paid before final assessment, often by instalments.
Payers must remit on time, file returns and issue withholding certificates.

en.title: Tax incentives and investment
en.short: Tax holidays, pioneer status, free zones and accelerated allowances: design, cost and effectiveness.

sections.heading: What incentives do
sections.text:
A tax incentive is a special tax rule meant to attract investment. A tax holiday exempts qualifying profits from income tax for a set period. Pioneer or special status is a legal designation granting such relief to approved industries. A free zone is a defined area where firms, often exporters, get customs and tax relief.

An investment allowance gives an extra deduction for qualifying capital spending. An accelerated capital allowance lets a firm deduct capital costs faster than normal. All are tax expenditures: they cost revenue like a grant, but without cash payment.

sections.heading: Country rules
sections.text:
Rules are country-specific and change. In Nigeria, pioneer status applications are processed by the Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission and approved by the Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment, and free zones are administered by the Nigeria Export Processing Zones Authority. Ghana, Kenya and South Africa also use special economic zones and targeted reliefs.

Eligibility, duration and conditions differ. Check current statute, regulations and official guidance from the tax authority and investment promotion agency.

sections.heading: Cost and effectiveness
sections.text:
Incentives can raise investment, but they cost revenue and can be poorly targeted. A holiday may reward projects that would have gone ahead, encourage profit shifting and invite lobbying. Free zones can become enclaves with weak local links.

Accelerated allowances mainly defer tax, so their present-value cost is smaller than an exemption. Effectiveness improves with clear eligibility, time limits, published cost estimates, monitoring and review. The test is additionality: what investment would not have happened without the incentive?

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Assume a 30% tax rate. A firm buys equipment for 100 million. Normal allowance is 10% a year, or 10 million. An accelerated allowance of 50% gives 50 million in year one. Extra deduction = 50 − 10 = 40 million. First-year tax saving = 40 × 30% = 12 million. Total allowances are unchanged, so the gain is mainly timing.

A five-year holiday on taxable profit of 20 million a year saves 20 × 30% × 5 = 30 million, but only if the investment is truly extra.

keyPoints: Tax incentives are tax expenditures: they reduce revenue and need cost-benefit review.
A tax holiday exempts profits for a set period; pioneer or special status is a statutory route to such relief.
Free zones give customs and tax relief, usually tied to location and export activity.
Investment allowances give an extra deduction; accelerated capital allowances bring deductions forward.
First-year saving from an extra allowance = extra deduction × tax rate.
Holiday saving = annual taxable profit × tax rate × holiday years, but only extra investment counts.

en.title: Tax audits, assessments and dispute resolution
en.short: How tax audits are selected, assessments made, objections and appeals handled, and penalties settled.

sections.heading: Audit selection and powers
sections.text: Revenue authorities use risk profiles to choose audits: unusual margins, large refunds, cash businesses, third-party data or random checks. An audit is an examination of records to test whether tax was correctly reported. Officials usually have powers to request books, invoices, bank statements and contracts, to interview staff and to inspect business premises. Powers and time limits are set by each country’s law, so check the local statute. Keep records for the period the law requires; in many countries this is several years after the return.

sections.heading: Assessment and objection
sections.text: Most systems rely on self-assessment: the taxpayer files a return and pays. The authority may accept it, adjust it after audit, or issue a best-judgement or additional assessment if no return is filed or records are poor. The taxpayer receives a notice stating the tax and reasons. If the taxpayer disagrees, it files a notice of objection within the statutory period, giving grounds and supporting documents. Many laws require payment of the undisputed amount while the dispute continues.

sections.heading: Appeals, penalties and settlement
sections.text: If the objection fails, the taxpayer may appeal to a tribunal and then to the courts. In Nigeria, federal tax disputes may go to the Tax Appeal Tribunal and afterwards to the courts; state procedures differ. Penalties and interest commonly apply for late filing, late payment and incorrect returns. Settlement or alternative dispute resolution may be allowed, but it cannot excuse a criminal offence. A concrete case: a trader keeps two sales ledgers. That is deliberate concealment, not an honest error.

sections.heading: Evasion, avoidance and error
sections.text: Tax evasion is illegal: deliberately hiding income or falsifying records. Tax avoidance uses the law to reduce tax, often by arranging affairs in a way the legislature did not intend; it is generally legal but anti-avoidance rules may cancel the benefit. An honest error is an unintentional mistake, such as a transposed figure, and is usually corrected with lower or no penalty. The boundary depends on intent and evidence, and procedures differ by country.

keyPoints: Audits are usually selected using risk profiles and third-party data, not only at random.
Taxpayers must keep records for the period set by local law and produce them when required.
A self-assessment can be adjusted; if no return is filed, the authority may issue a best-judgement assessment.
An objection must be filed within the statutory period and usually state grounds and evidence.
Evasion is deliberate and criminal; avoidance is legal arranging that anti-avoidance rules may challenge; honest error is unintentional.
Penalties and interest vary by country, and settlement cannot excuse evasion.

en.title: Tax planning and anti-avoidance
en.short: Legitimate planning through timing, entity, reliefs and financing, plus anti-avoidance rules and ethics.

sections.heading: Legitimate planning
sections.text: Tax planning means arranging your affairs, before a transaction, to reduce tax within the law. Four common levers are timing, entity choice, reliefs and financing. Timing shifts income or deductions between periods. Entity choice compares a sole trader, partnership and company, whose rates and compliance duties differ. Reliefs are allowances, loss reliefs or incentives that meet stated conditions. Financing compares debt, where interest may be deductible, with equity, where dividends usually are not. A plan should have a commercial reason beyond tax.

sections.heading: Avoidance and rules
sections.text: Tax avoidance is legal but uses the letter of the law to defeat its purpose. Tax evasion is illegal: it involves concealment, false records or non-disclosure. Countries use specific anti-avoidance rules for known schemes, such as thin capitalisation (excessive debt funding), transfer pricing and disguised remuneration. A general anti-avoidance rule (GAAR) is broader: it lets the revenue authority disregard or recharacterise an arrangement whose main purpose is a tax benefit and which lacks substance. Substance means genuine commercial activity, risk and purpose. South Africa and the UK have GAARs. Nigeria has anti-avoidance provisions in its tax statutes; check the current text and guidance.

sections.heading: Worked example: debt or equity
sections.text: A company needs 1,000,000 and pays tax at 30%. It can borrow at 10% interest or issue equity. Debt: interest is 1,000,000 × 10% = 100,000. If interest is deductible, tax falls by 100,000 × 30% = 30,000, so the after-tax cost is 70,000. Equity: a dividend of 100,000 is usually not deductible, so the company bears 100,000. Debt looks cheaper, but thin capitalisation or interest-limitation rules may deny the deduction if debt is excessive.

sections.heading: Ethics and practice
sections.text: Ethics goes beyond legality. An arrangement may be legal yet damage trust, invite penalties or fail a professional code. Advisers should document commercial substance, avoid misleading the revenue authority and advise clients on risk. If a scheme depends on a strained reading of the law, say so. The test is not only whether it works, but whether it is defensible and fair.

keyPoints: Tax planning is arranging affairs before a transaction to reduce tax within the law, with a commercial reason.
Timing, entity choice, reliefs and financing are the main planning levers.
Tax avoidance is legal but contrary to legislative purpose; tax evasion is illegal.
Specific anti-avoidance rules target known schemes; a GAAR can recharacterise arrangements lacking substance.
Interest deductibility can make debt cheaper than equity: tax saving = deductible interest × tax rate.
Legal is not always ethical; document substance and check the current country law.

en.title: International taxation: residence, source and double taxation
en.short: Residence and source rules, double taxation, treaties, foreign tax credits and permanent establishment.

sections.heading: Residence and source
sections.text: Residence and source decide which country may tax income. Residence is the taxpayer’s legal link to a country. For individuals it usually depends on days present, domicile or other ties; a few countries, such as the United States, also use citizenship. For companies, it depends on incorporation or place of effective management. Source is where income arises, such as where work is done. Residents are commonly taxed on worldwide income; non-residents only on local-source income. Rules differ by country, so check domestic law and the treaty.

sections.heading: Double taxation and treaties
sections.text: Double taxation means the same income is taxed twice. Juridical double taxation is one person taxed by two countries on the same income. Economic double taxation is the same income taxed in two persons’ hands, such as a company and its shareholder. Tax treaties divide taxing rights and give relief. The OECD Model Convention mainly protects residence-country rights. The UN Model Convention gives more rights to source countries, which many developing countries prefer. Treaties also define residence and permanent establishment.

sections.heading: Foreign tax credit
sections.text: Relief may be a credit, exemption or deduction. A credit subtracts foreign tax from domestic tax on the same income, usually capped at the domestic tax on that income. Suppose a Country A company earns 100,000 in Country B. B taxes it at 20%, so 20,000 is paid. A taxes worldwide income at 30%, giving 30,000 before relief. Credit 20,000, so A tax payable is 10,000. Total tax 30,000. If B taxed 35,000, credit is usually capped at 30,000; excess relief depends on A’s rules.

sections.heading: Permanent establishment and shopping
sections.text: A permanent establishment (PE) is a fixed place of business through which a company carries on business in another country. It may also arise through a dependent agent, a person who habitually concludes contracts for the company in that country. A PE lets the source country tax attributable profits. Treaty shopping means arranging affairs to obtain treaty benefits, such as lower withholding tax on dividends, interest or royalties, that the real owner would not otherwise get. Countries counter it with anti-abuse rules such as the principal purpose test in the OECD Multilateral Instrument. Check the treaty and domestic law.

keyPoints: Residence and source rules decide which country may tax an item; check domestic law and the treaty.
Juridical double taxation is one person taxed twice on the same income; economic double taxation is the same income taxed in two persons’ hands.
The OECD Model Convention favours residence-country taxing rights, while the UN Model Convention gives more rights to source countries.
Foreign tax credit = foreign tax paid, capped at domestic tax on the same income.
A permanent establishment is a fixed place of business or dependent agent that lets the source country tax attributable profits.
Treaty shopping uses treaty benefits the real owner would not otherwise get; anti-abuse rules such as the principal purpose test counter it.

en.title: Transfer pricing and related-party transactions
en.short: Arm’s length pricing, methods, comparables, documentation, penalties and disputes.

sections.heading: Arm’s length principle
sections.text: Transfer pricing is the price charged between related parties, such as a parent and subsidiary, for goods, services, loans or intangibles. The arm’s length principle, in Article 9 of the OECD Model Tax Convention and the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines, requires prices to match what independent parties would agree. OECD guidance is influential but not law; each country’s domestic rules and treaties govern. Rules differ, so check the current local regulations, such as Nigeria’s transfer pricing regulations.

sections.heading: Methods and comparables
sections.text: OECD guidance sets out five main methods. Comparable uncontrolled price uses a price between independent parties. Resale price deducts a normal margin from the resale price. Cost plus adds a normal mark-up to costs. Transactional net margin compares net profit with a base such as sales or costs. Profit split divides combined profit by contributions. The best method depends on facts. Comparables are reliable independent transactions or data, adjusted for differences.

sections.heading: Documentation and penalties
sections.text: Many countries require records proving arm’s length pricing. The OECD recommends a master file, local file and, for large groups, country-by-country report, but thresholds vary. Penalties for missing documentation or for a tax adjustment vary by country and may include fines, interest and extra tax. Good-faith documentation can reduce exposure. Check local deadlines and rules.

sections.heading: Disputes and example
sections.text: Disputes begin when an authority adjusts a price. Taxpayers may appeal domestically. Tax treaties may allow a mutual agreement procedure (MAP), where both authorities try to agree. Some treaties allow arbitration, and advance pricing arrangements (APAs) approve a method in advance. BEPS Action 14 aims to improve dispute resolution. Example: parent cost 70, independent price 100, subsidiary resale 130. At transfer price 100, each profit is 30. With Country A tax 30% and Country B 10%, total tax is 30% × 30 + 10% × 30 = 12. At price 80, profits are 10 and 50, tax is 3 + 5 = 8. The arm’s length price stops profit shifting.

keyPoints: Transfer pricing sets prices for transactions between related parties.
The arm’s length principle requires the price independent parties would agree.
The five OECD methods are comparable uncontrolled price, resale price, cost plus, transactional net margin and profit split.
Comparables are independent transactions or data adjusted for differences.
Documentation and penalties vary by country; the OECD recommends master file, local file and country-by-country reporting for large groups.
Tax effect equals tax rate × profit allocated to each country, and MAP, arbitration and APAs help resolve disputes.

en.title: Tax policy, public finance and reform
en.short: Revenue needs, incidence, efficiency, equity, tax expenditures, informality and reform choices.

sections.heading: Revenue, efficiency, equity
sections.text: Tax policy chooses what to tax, at what rate and with what reliefs. Public finance studies government revenue and spending. Revenue needs depend on planned public goods, transfers and debt service. Efficiency means raising a given revenue with the smallest excess burden, or deadweight loss: the welfare lost when taxes change behaviour. Equity asks who should bear the burden. Horizontal equity treats similar people alike; vertical equity asks those with greater ability to pay to pay more. Ability to pay and benefit received are rival principles, and governments trade them against efficiency.

sections.heading: Incidence example
sections.text:
Statutory incidence is who legally pays; economic incidence is who really bears the cost after prices adjust. In a competitive market the burden falls more on the less elastic side.

Example: Qd = 120 − P and Qs = 2P. Without tax, 120 − P = 2P, so P = 40 and Q = 80. A tax of 15 per unit on sellers changes supply to Qs = 2(P − 15). Then 120 − P = 2P − 30, so P = 50. Buyers pay 50, sellers keep 35. Buyer burden = 10; seller burden = 5. The 15 tax is shared.

sections.heading: Tax expenditures and informality
sections.text: Tax expenditures are revenue forgone through exemptions, deductions, credits or preferential rates. They are spending by another name, so good practice reports their cost. The informal sector covers firms and workers outside the tax net. Causes include low incomes, high compliance costs, weak enforcement and distrust. Common responses are simplified regimes, presumptive taxes based on turnover or assets, VAT thresholds and electronic payment trails. These can help, but must not punish poor small firms.

sections.heading: Reform choices
sections.text: Reform in developing countries often combines a broader base, simpler rules, stronger administration and credible public spending. Distributional analysis matters: a tax can look fair by law yet burden poor households through prices. Context differs, so no single package is universal. Check current official sources for rates, thresholds and rules.

keyPoints: Tax policy balances revenue needs against efficiency and equity.
Statutory incidence is who legally pays; economic incidence is who bears the burden after prices adjust.
In competitive markets, the less elastic side bears more of a tax.
Buyer burden = price paid after tax − price before tax; seller burden = tax − buyer burden.
Tax expenditures are revenue forgone through reliefs and should be reported and reviewed.
Informal-sector policy often uses simplified or presumptive taxes, but design must protect the poor.

en.title: Property, wealth and transaction taxes
en.short: Annual property taxes, stamp duty, inheritance and wealth taxes, and how values are assessed.

sections.heading: Annual property taxes
sections.text: Property tax is an annual tax on ownership or occupation of real property, usually collected by local government. Land rates are a form, charged on the assessed value of land and buildings. Examples include municipal property rates in South Africa under the Municipal Property Rates Act 2004, council tax in England, Scotland and Wales for homes, and land use charge in Lagos State, Nigeria. The tax base is assessed value, either capital value (market value) or rental value. A valuation roll lists properties and values. Administration involves assessment, billing, collection and appeals. Rates vary; check current local law.

sections.heading: Transaction and transfer taxes
sections.text: Stamp duty is a tax on written instruments, such as deeds transferring land or shares. In England and Northern Ireland, Stamp Duty Land Tax applies to property purchases; Scotland and Wales have their own land transaction taxes. In Nigeria, stamp duty is imposed under the Stamp Duties Act. Capital transfer tax is a tax on transfers of capital, during life or at death; the United Kingdom used it from 1975 to 1986 before replacing it with inheritance tax. Estate or inheritance taxes apply at death: an estate tax is levied on the estate, an inheritance tax on the recipient. Many countries, including Nigeria and Canada, have no inheritance tax, though other taxes may apply. Net wealth taxes are annual taxes on assets minus debts above a threshold; they exist in a few countries such as Switzerland (cantonal), Norway and Spain, but are rare. Rates and thresholds differ; check current law.

sections.heading: Valuation and worked case
sections.text: Valuation estimates property value for tax. Common bases are market value, replacement cost and rental value. A cadastre or land registry records ownership and boundaries. For illustration only, suppose a local rate is 0.6% of assessed value and stamp duty on a transfer is 1.5%. A property assessed at 5,000,000 is charged 5,000,000 × 0.006 = 30,000 per year. On sale, stamp duty is 5,000,000 × 0.015 = 75,000. These rates are hypothetical; actual rates vary by country and year.

keyPoints: Property tax is usually an annual local tax on assessed property value; land rates are one form.
Stamp duty is charged on written instruments such as property or share transfers, and rates vary by country.
Estate and inheritance taxes apply at death, while net wealth taxes are annual taxes on assets minus debts above a threshold.
Annual property tax = assessed value × rate; stamp duty = transfer value × rate.
Valuation may use market, rental or replacement cost bases, and a cadastre or valuation roll supports administration.
Check the current law of the relevant country, because rates, thresholds and reliefs differ.

en.title: Customs and excise duties: imports, valuation and trade rules
en.short: Customs and excise duties: imports, classification, valuation, origin, excise goods, smuggling and trade agreements.

sections.heading: Duties and classification
sections.text: Customs duty is a tax on goods crossing a border, usually imports; export duty is less common. Excise duty is a tax on selected goods, such as alcohol, tobacco and fuel, whether made locally or imported. Classification places goods in the Harmonized System (HS), maintained by the World Customs Organization. The HS uses six-digit codes; countries add digits. The code sets the tariff rate and any controls. In Nigeria, the Nigeria Customs Service applies the ECOWAS Common External Tariff. Rates and rules change, so check the current official tariff.

sections.heading: Valuation and origin
sections.text: Customs value is the base for ad valorem duty, a duty charged as a percentage of value. Most WTO members use transaction value: the price actually paid or payable, adjusted for freight, insurance and certain costs. Some countries use CIF (cost, insurance, freight); others use FOB (free on board). Rules of origin decide the country a good comes from for preferential rates under trade agreements. Origin is not the same as where goods were shipped from.

sections.heading: Excise and trade
sections.text: Excise goods are controlled because they raise revenue or discourage harm. Smuggling is moving goods across a border without paying duty or obeying controls; penalties include seizure and prosecution. Trade agreements reduce duties for members. Examples are the ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme, which cuts duties on goods traded within ECOWAS, the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and the EU customs union. Each has its own origin rules and schedules.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A made-up import has customs value (CIF) of $10,000. The tariff rate is 20% and excise is 10% of the duty-inclusive value. Customs duty = 10,000 × 20% = $2,000. Value for excise = 10,000 + 2,000 = $12,000. Excise = 12,000 × 10% = $1,200. Total duty and excise = $3,200. Check: 10,000 × 1.20 × 1.10 = 13,200; tax = 3,200. This is illustrative; actual bases and rates vary by country.

keyPoints: Customs duty is a tax on imports or exports; excise duty is a tax on selected goods such as alcohol, tobacco and fuel.
The HS code sets the tariff rate, and countries add digits to the six-digit WCO code.
Customs value is usually transaction value, adjusted; check whether the country uses CIF or FOB.
Rules of origin decide preferential tariff treatment under trade agreements.
Customs duty = customs value × tariff rate; excise may be charged on the duty-inclusive value.
Smuggling is evasion of customs controls and can lead to seizure and prosecution.

en.title: Taxation of the digital economy
en.short: Nexus, withholding, digital services taxes, VAT on digital supplies and the OECD two-pillar plan.

sections.heading: Why digital trade is hard to tax
sections.text:
The digital economy covers e-commerce, apps, streaming, cloud services, online advertising and platforms. A firm can earn from customers in a country without offices, staff or stock there. Corporate tax relies on nexus, the connection that gives a country the right to tax. Treaties often require a permanent establishment (PE), such as a fixed place. Digital sales may create no PE, so the source country may tax nothing.

Countries such as Nigeria use wider nexus tests, such as significant economic presence (SEP), a taxable connection based on sales or users rather than a fixed place. They also apply withholding taxes on digital payments. Withholding is tax collected by the payer and remitted to the tax authority, usually on gross amounts. Treaties may reduce it.

sections.heading: Digital services taxes
sections.text:
Some countries levy a digital services tax (DST) on gross revenue from digital activities. Examples include France and the United Kingdom; India uses an equalisation levy on some online payments to non-residents. DSTs often target large non-resident groups and are controversial because they tax revenue, not profit.

Rates and scope change, so check current law. DSTs sit outside the OECD/G20 two-pillar project, though the deal is meant to replace them once Pillar One takes effect.

sections.heading: VAT on digital supplies
sections.text:
VAT on digital supplies follows the destination principle: tax is due where the consumer is. Many countries require non-resident suppliers to register and remit VAT, often through a simplified online system. The EU one-stop shop is an example. For business-to-business sales, the reverse charge may apply: the customer accounts for the VAT instead of the supplier.

Suppose a non-resident supplier sells an app to a consumer for 100 before VAT and the destination rate is 16%. VAT = 100 × 16% = 16. The customer pays 116 and the supplier remits 16. If 100 is VAT-inclusive, VAT = 100 × 16 ÷ 116 = 13.79.

sections.heading: OECD two-pillar approach
sections.text:
Pillar One reallocates taxing rights to market countries for the largest multinational groups and simplifies some transfer pricing. Pillar Two sets a global minimum effective tax rate of 15% for large groups, generally those with revenue above €750 million. It uses top-up taxes under the GloBE rules.

Implementation differs by country and is still developing. Check current official sources.

keyPoints: Digital firms can create nexus without physical presence, so PE rules may fail.
Withholding tax is collected at source on gross payments and may be reduced by treaties.
DSTs tax gross digital revenue and are unilateral and controversial.
VAT on digital supplies is due where the consumer is, and non-resident suppliers may register and remit.
Pillar One reallocates taxing rights; Pillar Two sets a 15% global minimum effective tax rate for large groups.
Rules and rates change by country and year, so check official sources.

en.title: Taxation of natural resources
en.short: Petroleum and mining fiscal regimes, royalties, production sharing, rent taxes, stability and environment.

sections.heading: Fiscal regimes
sections.text: Natural resources are taxed through a fiscal regime: the package of royalties, taxes, state participation and production sharing. A royalty is a payment based on gross production or value, usually before costs. Mining regimes usually combine a royalty, corporate income tax and sometimes state equity. A production sharing contract (PSC) lets a contractor recover costs from cost oil or cost gas, then share profit oil with the state. A resource rent tax targets economic rent: profit above a normal return. Countries mix these tools. In Nigeria, upstream petroleum is governed by the Petroleum Industry Act 2021 and mining by the Minerals and Mining Act 2007. Rates and terms change, so check the current law and regulator.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Illustrative PSC, not a country’s rates. Gross revenue is $100 million. Royalty at 10% is $10 million, leaving $90 million. Recoverable cost is $40 million. Cost recovery is capped at 50% of revenue after royalty, which is $45 million, so the full $40 million is recovered. Profit oil is $90m − $40m = $50m. Split 60% to the state and 40% to the contractor: state $30m, contractor $20m. The contractor also pays tax on its share. Total government take before tax is royalty $10m + state profit oil $30m = $40m, or 40% of gross revenue. Check: 10 + 30 = 40; 40 ÷ 100 = 40%.

sections.heading: Stability and environment
sections.text: Fiscal stability clauses aim to protect investors from changed tax terms, but they can limit a country’s future revenue and may be renegotiated. Environmental issues include decommissioning and abandonment costs, spills, water use and land rehabilitation. Governments use environmental bonds, trust funds or tax deductions for approved decommissioning. Royalties can discourage marginal projects, while rent taxes can be progressive.

keyPoints: A fiscal regime is the full set of royalties, taxes, state participation and production sharing.
A royalty is normally charged on gross value before cost recovery.
In a PSC, cost recovery is usually capped, then profit oil is shared between state and contractor.
A resource rent tax targets profit above a normal return.
Government take = royalty + state profit share + taxes.
Rates and rules are country-specific; check current law, such as Nigeria’s PIA 2021.

en.title: Local government taxation and fiscal federalism
en.short: Local taxes, rates, revenue assignment, transfers and local administration in a federal system.

sections.heading: Fiscal federalism
sections.text: Fiscal federalism is the division of taxing powers and spending duties among levels of government. It aims to match revenue with responsibilities. A vertical gap arises when a level spends more than it can raise; a horizontal gap is the difference between rich and poor areas. Nigeria’s 1999 Constitution (as amended) assigns major taxes to the federal government, some to states, and local rates and fees to local government councils. Other countries divide powers differently, so always check the constitution and current statutes.

sections.heading: Local taxes and rates
sections.text: Local governments in Nigeria may collect rates, fees, charges and levies. The Fourth Schedule to the Constitution lists their functions, including collection of rates and assessment of privately owned houses for rates prescribed by the State House of Assembly. A rate is a property tax, often called a tenement rate, charged as a percentage of assessed value. Levies and fees are payments for services or permits, such as market stalls, motor parks, signboards and refuse collection. Local councils do not levy personal or company income tax; those are assigned to other levels.

sections.heading: Transfers and administration
sections.text: Intergovernmental transfers are grants from higher to lower levels. In Nigeria, local governments receive statutory allocations from the Federation Account and from state governments. Section 162 of the Constitution requires each state to maintain a State Joint Local Government Account for these funds. Transfers reduce fiscal gaps but can bring state control and delay. Local administration covers assessment, collection, budgeting and accountability. Weak capacity and leakages are common problems, so transparent records and audits matter.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Suppose a state prescribes a rate of 0.5% and a house is assessed at ₦20,000,000. The annual rate is 20,000,000 × 0.005 = ₦100,000. For transfers, suppose a state receives ₦100 million for 10 councils and shares 60% equally. The shared amount is 100,000,000 × 0.60 = ₦60,000,000. Each council gets 60,000,000 ÷ 10 = ₦6,000,000. These figures are illustrative; actual rates and sharing formulas are set by law.

keyPoints: Fiscal federalism assigns taxing and spending powers among levels of government.
In Nigeria, local governments collect property rates, fees and levies under the Fourth Schedule to the 1999 Constitution.
Income tax is not a local government tax in Nigeria; it is assigned to federal and state governments.
Intergovernmental transfers, including statutory allocations, aim to close vertical and horizontal fiscal gaps.
The State Joint Local Government Account is the constitutional channel for local government allocations in Nigeria.
Property rate = assessed value × prescribed rate; check current state law for the rate.

en.title: Tax ethics and professional conduct
en.short: Duties, confidentiality, conflicts, client money, aggressive avoidance, whistleblowing and professional codes.

sections.heading: Duties and standards
sections.text: A tax practitioner acts for a client but also owes duties to the tax system and the public. Core standards are integrity, objectivity, confidentiality, professional competence and due care, and professional behaviour. In Nigeria, the Chartered Institute of Taxation of Nigeria (CITN) and the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria (ICAN) publish codes for members. Many bodies also use the International Ethics Standards Board for Accountants (IESBA) Code. Practitioners must not sign a return they know is false or mislead a tax authority.

sections.heading: Confidentiality and conflicts
sections.text: Confidentiality means not disclosing client information without authority, except where law requires or permits. A conflict of interest arises when the practitioner’s own interest, or another client’s interest, could affect advice. The practitioner should identify it, disclose it, obtain informed consent where possible, or decline the work. Client money must be kept in a separate client account, never mixed with the firm’s money, and recorded accurately.

sections.heading: Avoidance and whistleblowing
sections.text: Tax planning uses the law to reduce tax. Tax evasion is illegal. Aggressive avoidance may be lawful but can be abusive, and it may attract penalties or reputational harm. A practitioner should test whether a scheme has commercial substance and should not promote one without a reasonable legal basis. Whistleblowing means reporting wrongdoing. Confidentiality does not always prevent reporting a crime, but the rules differ by country; check the applicable code and law.

sections.heading: Case: Adaeze in Lagos
sections.text: Adaeze, a tax adviser in Lagos, discovers that a client has left sales out of a return. She must not sign the return. She explains the risk and asks the client to correct it. If the client refuses, she should consider withdrawing and, under the applicable Nigerian rules and law, reporting the matter. She keeps any client refund in a separate client account.

keyPoints: Integrity and objectivity come before the client’s wishes.
Confidentiality is limited by law and by the professional code.
Conflicts of interest must be disclosed and managed, or the engagement declined.
Client money belongs in a separate client account, not the firm’s account.
Aggressive avoidance is not evasion, but it needs a reasonable legal basis.
Whistleblowing rules vary by country, so check the code and the law.

en.title: Tax in financial statements: current and deferred tax
en.short: Current tax, deferred tax, temporary differences, tax base and IAS 12 disclosure.

sections.heading: Current tax and tax base
sections.text:
Current tax is tax payable or refundable on taxable profit for the period. It follows the country’s tax law, not accounting rules. Taxable profit starts from accounting profit and adjusts for differences such as disallowed expenses and tax depreciation. Current tax = taxable profit × tax rate, subject to credits and reliefs.

The tax base is the amount attributed to an asset or liability for tax purposes. For an asset, it is the amount deductible for tax in future periods. For a liability, it is carrying amount minus future tax deduction. It differs from accounting carrying amount.

sections.heading: Deferred tax
sections.text:
A temporary difference is carrying amount minus tax base. A taxable temporary difference (carrying amount above tax base) creates a deferred tax liability, because future taxable amounts arise. A deductible temporary difference (carrying amount below tax base) creates a deferred tax asset, because future deductions arise.

Deferred tax estimates future tax from these differences. Deferred tax = temporary difference × expected tax rate. A deferred tax asset is recognised only if taxable profit is probable. Current tax is recognised as income or expense, except when it arises from items in other comprehensive income or equity.
