IAS 12 measures deferred tax at enacted or substantively enacted rates expected on reversal, without discounting. US GAAP ASC 740 is comparable but not identical.

sections.heading: Worked example and disclosure
sections.text:
Example, first year. A machine costs 100,000. Accounting depreciation is 20,000; tax depreciation is 30,000. Profit before tax is 200,000. Tax rate is 25%.

Carrying amount = 100,000 − 20,000 = 80,000.
Tax base = 100,000 − 30,000 = 70,000.
Taxable temporary difference = 80,000 − 70,000 = 10,000.
DTL = 10,000 × 25% = 2,500.
Taxable profit = 200,000 + 20,000 − 30,000 = 190,000.
Current tax = 190,000 × 25% = 47,500.
Tax expense = 47,500 + 2,500 = 50,000.

Disclosure shows tax expense components, a tax reconciliation and deferred tax movements.

keyPoints: Current tax = taxable profit × tax rate, using country tax law.
Tax base of an asset is the future tax deduction; for a liability it is carrying amount minus future tax deduction.
A taxable temporary difference creates a deferred tax liability.
A deductible temporary difference creates a deferred tax asset, recognised only if taxable profit is probable.
Deferred tax = temporary difference × expected tax rate, using enacted or substantively enacted rates.
Disclose tax expense components, tax reconciliation and deferred tax movements under IAS 12.

en.title: Tax research and technical writing
en.short: Finding tax law, reading judgments, using citators, and writing a referenced tax memo.

sections.heading: Finding the law
sections.text: Start with primary authority: the statute, regulations made under it, and court decisions. Use the official gazette or official legislation website for the text, and the tax authority’s website for official guidance. Guidance explains how the authority applies the law, but it is not the law itself and can change. Secondary sources such as textbooks and journal articles help you understand, but cite them only as support. Record the full citation and the date you accessed online material.

sections.heading: Reading judgments
sections.text: A judgment is a court’s reasoned decision. Find the court, date, procedural history, facts, issue, holding and reasoning. The ratio decidendi is the legal rule necessary to the decision; it can bind lower courts in the same jurisdiction. Obiter dicta are remarks not necessary to the decision; they persuade but do not bind. Check whether the court distinguished, followed or overruled earlier cases. Do not quote a sentence without its context.

sections.heading: Citators and currency
sections.text: A citator is an index that shows later cases and articles citing a case or statute. It flags treatment such as followed, distinguished, doubted or overruled. Use one before relying on any case. Tax law changes often, so confirm that the provision is in force and that later amendments have not altered it. State the law as at a clear date. If official guidance has been replaced, cite the current version and say so.

sections.heading: Writing the memo
sections.text: Use a standard structure: issue, facts, law, analysis and conclusion. For example, if a client asks whether a payment is deductible, cite the provision, a case applying it and current guidance, then apply them to the facts. Cite every authority you rely on and disclose contrary authority. Use a recognised citation style, such as OSCOLA in the United Kingdom, or the style your school or firm requires. Never invent a citation. Keep client information confidential, and do not copy another writer’s words without quotation and attribution.

keyPoints: Start from primary authority: statutes, regulations and court decisions, with official guidance as an explanation of how the authority applies the law.
The ratio decidendi binds lower courts in the same jurisdiction; obiter dicta are persuasive only.
A citator shows how later cases have treated an authority, so use one before relying on a case.
Tax law changes, so state the date of your research and confirm that the provision and guidance are current.
A tax memo normally follows issue, facts, law, analysis and conclusion.
Cite every source accurately, disclose contrary authority, and never invent or misquote a citation.

en.title: Advanced tax theory and policy
en.short: Optimal taxation, incidence, behavioural responses, tax competition and the equity-efficiency trade-off.

sections.heading: Framing the problem
sections.text:
Tax policy judges a tax by revenue, equity, efficiency and administrability. Statutory incidence names who legally pays; economic incidence names who bears the burden. A tax on sellers may shift forward to buyers or backward to workers and owners. The split depends on elasticities: the less elastic side bears more.

Equity concerns fair treatment of similar people (horizontal) and different capacities (vertical). Efficiency concerns excess burden, the deadweight loss from changed behaviour. Excess burden rises with the square of the tax rate and with elasticities, so high rates on responsive bases are costly.

sections.heading: Optimal tax schools
sections.text:
Welfarist optimal tax theory, associated with Ramsey and Mirrlees, chooses taxes to maximise a social welfare function subject to revenue. It trades equity against efficiency and may tax less elastic bases more heavily, but conclusions depend on welfare weights (how much society values gains to different groups) and labour supply responses. Rawlsian versions weight the worst off most.

Public choice theory stresses government failure, lobbying and rent-seeking, so it favours simple broad bases. Supply-side and libertarian arguments emphasise lower marginal rates and limited government. These schools disagree on values and on government behaviour, so no policy prescription follows without stating those assumptions.

sections.heading: Evidence and competition
sections.text:
Empirical work estimates behavioural responses: taxable income elasticities, bunching at kink points (clustering of taxpayers where tax rates change), labour supply, saving and investment. Incidence studies examine whether taxes pass into prices or wages.

Tax competition arises when mobile capital or skilled labour moves to lower-tax jurisdictions. Theory predicts pressure on capital taxes; evidence is mixed, and small open economies differ from large ones. Policy conclusions are conditional on mobility, enforcement capacity and public spending needs.

sections.heading: A simple case
sections.text:
Take demand Q = 100 − P and supply Q = P, with a unit tax of 10 on sellers. Supply becomes Q = P − 10. Equating 100 − P = P − 10 gives P = 55. Buyers pay 55 instead of 50, sellers receive 45.

The tax is shared equally: 5 each. If demand were less elastic, buyers would bear more.

keyPoints: Statutory incidence is legal liability; economic incidence is the final burden.
The less elastic side of a market bears more of a tax.
Excess burden rises with the square of the tax rate and with elasticities.
Optimal tax theory trades equity against efficiency and depends on welfare weights.
Empirical evidence uses taxable income elasticities and bunching at kinks.
Tax competition conclusions depend on mobility and enforcement capacity.

en.title: Advanced international taxation
en.short: Treaty interpretation, BEPS, transfer pricing, disputes, digital economy and developing countries.

sections.heading: Treaty interpretation
sections.text: Tax treaties are bilateral agreements based on the OECD or UN Model. They divide taxing rights and relieve double taxation. Interpretation follows the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties: ordinary meaning in context, object and purpose. The OECD and UN Commentaries are persuasive, not binding. Country practice differs: OECD members often follow the OECD Model, while many developing countries use the UN Model, which keeps more source-country taxing rights. Always read the treaty text and reservations.

sections.heading: BEPS and transfer pricing
sections.text: BEPS means base erosion and profit shifting: multinational groups exploit gaps and mismatches in tax rules to move profit to low-tax places. The OECD/G20 BEPS project has 15 Actions. Minimum standards cover harmful tax practices, treaty abuse, country-by-country reporting and dispute resolution. The Multilateral Instrument implements many treaty measures. Transfer pricing applies the arm’s length principle: related parties price as independent parties would. Advanced work uses comparables, profit splits and the DEMPE functions for intangibles: development, enhancement, maintenance, protection and exploitation. A simple check: if a comparable markup on cost is 10% and cost is 100,000, the arm’s length price is 100,000 × 1.10 = 110,000, giving profit of 10,000.

sections.heading: Disputes and digital economy
sections.text: Dispute resolution uses the mutual agreement procedure (MAP), where competent authorities negotiate. Advance pricing agreements (APAs) agree pricing in advance. Arbitration is available only where the treaty provides it. The digital economy challenges physical-presence rules. The OECD two-pillar solution reallocates some taxing rights to market countries (Pillar One) and sets a 15% global minimum tax for large groups (Pillar Two), subject to country implementation.

sections.heading: Developing countries
sections.text: Developing countries often rely on the UN Model, withholding taxes and simplified approaches. Capacity limits make complex rules hard to administer. Country practice and implementation dates vary, so check current official OECD and UN materials and local law.

keyPoints: Tax treaties divide taxing rights and are interpreted under the Vienna Convention.
OECD and UN Commentaries are persuasive, not binding.
BEPS minimum standards cover harmful practices, treaty abuse, CbCR and disputes.
Transfer pricing follows the arm’s length principle, with DEMPE guiding intangible profits.
MAP and APAs resolve disputes; arbitration depends on the treaty.
Pillar One and Pillar Two respond to the digital economy, but implementation varies by country.

en.title: Research methods for taxation
en.short: Designing legal and empirical tax research, from data and analysis to ethics and writing.

sections.heading: Research design and question
sections.text: Start with a clear research question, not a topic. A question such as 'Why do small firms under-report VAT in Lagos State, Nigeria?' can be answered with evidence. Research design is the plan linking question, methods, data and conclusion. It may be doctrinal (studying legal rules), empirical (using observations), or mixed. A literature review shows what is known and defines key terms. A hypothesis is a testable statement; in qualitative work, a proposition or theme may replace it.

sections.heading: Legal and empirical methods
sections.text: Legal method, also called doctrinal method, reads primary sources: legislation, regulations, case law and official guidance. It asks what the law says and how it is interpreted. Empirical method studies what happens in practice using surveys, interviews, experiments or administrative records. For the Lagos question, legal method examines the charging rules and penalties; empirical method measures reported and unreported VAT. Triangulation means using more than one source to strengthen a finding.

sections.heading: Data and analysis
sections.text: Data sources include tax statutes, court judgments, tax authority publications, national statistics, firm accounts, surveys and interviews. Quantitative analysis uses numbers: descriptive statistics, regression or difference-in-differences (comparing changes in a treated group with a control group). Qualitative analysis uses interviews and documents to identify themes and explanations. A simple mixed design could compare audit records with interviews. Check data quality, sample bias and confidentiality. Do not claim causation from correlation alone.

sections.heading: Ethics and dissertation writing
sections.text: Ethics require informed consent, anonymity, secure storage and compliance with data protection law. Tax data are sensitive; never identify a taxpayer without permission. Avoid plagiarism and declare funding or conflicts. Dissertation writing follows a structure: introduction, literature review, methodology, findings, discussion, conclusion and references. The methodology must explain choices and limits so another researcher could repeat the study.

keyPoints: A tax research question should be answerable with evidence, not just a broad topic.
Doctrinal method analyses legislation, case law and official guidance; empirical method studies practice.
Mixed methods combine legal analysis with surveys, interviews or administrative data.
Quantitative analysis tests patterns with numbers; qualitative analysis explains meanings and behaviour.
Ethics require consent, anonymity, secure data and avoidance of plagiarism.
A dissertation must report methods and limits clearly enough to be repeated.
